scope: Seventh expansion batch: 27 exercises on the remaining temporal nouns. Six uchi items cover acting before a change and a change developing during activity; six aida items contrast explicit interval-topic and within-interval framing; six toki/koro items contrast neutral time reference with explicitly approximate framing; three tabi items mark each occurrence; six occasion-reference items share toki/ori/sai, with three ori and three sai model options. Shared accepted forms are not independently discriminated targets.

sources.publisher: The Japan Foundation, Minna no Kyozai
sources.section: Uchi ni / nai uchi ni: inspected the raw HTML structure chart, explanations A-C and examples 1-12. Supports noun/adjective/plain-verb attachment, before-change windows, negative before-event uses and changes developing during activity. Teacher-note categorical restrictions on negative aida are not adopted.

sources.publisher: The Japan Foundation, Japanese-Language Education Newsletter
sources.section: Expression intentions: time (2), sections 1-2. Aida ni and uchi ni locate activity within a period; aida wa and uchi wa present the period topically, often with contrast to afterward. The cooking/painting dialogues and parallel formulations explicitly show overlapping expressions. Used for requested discourse framing, not a universal ungrammaticality rule based on event duration.
Toki: sections 2-3 and 5-7. Relative timing, adjective/noun attachment, optional ni, and nonpast descriptions at past reference times. Does not restrict toki to exact instants or brief periods.

Koro noun sense 1; goro suffix sense 1; usage comparison koro/ori/sai/setsu. Supports approximate periods, the time-expression suffix, and the overlap of ori and sai for action occasions. The comparison itself gives an ori/sai substitution example; it does not establish universal equivalence.

Tabi ni explanation: each occurrence of an action/event and comparison with goto ni. Raw HTML Structure section specifies dictionary-form verb + tabi ni or noun + no + tabi ni; independently inspected during review.

Sai ni attachment after dictionary/past verbs and noun + no. Used for the illustrated occasion constructions; broad assertions about importance, ordinary events and one-off situations are not imported as categorical restrictions.

Komu, heading komu/komu/komu and sense 1 (be crowded): reviewer inspected the raw HTML entry 込む／混む／籠む and its supplement identifying 混む as a frequent, not exclusive, spelling of this sense. Supports accepting 込まない alongside the preferred 混まない.

authoringNotes: All scenarios are newly authored. The sources support grammatical functions and attachment; exact examples, translations, accepted answers and distractors require independent linguistic review.
All 68 prior exercise records remain unchanged. Each new exercise has one SRS identity; choose/type presentations and accepted spelling variants do not add exercises.

Uchi tasks visibly restrict the supplied verb to nai or te-iru forms. Accept kana spellings and te-ru/de-ru contractions. Do not claim dictionary-form uchi, affirmative state windows, mae or aida paraphrases are globally wrong.

Aida tasks include the particle in the blank and explicitly ask for either interval-as-topic framing with wa or within-interval framing with ni. Their exclusion rationale is that requested construction, not a false rule that a single event forbids wa or that ni forbids all durative predicates.

Toki/koro tasks visibly ask for either no added approximation or explicit approximate-time framing. Both can otherwise fit memories and plans. The long student-period toki item and short arrival-window koro item guard against a short-versus-long shortcut.

Occasion questions visibly restrict the noun list to tabi/toki/ori/sai. All six occasion-reference items accept kana and kanji for toki, ori and sai, with no competing equivalent button. Tabi items explicitly ask for each-occurrence quantification in the noun itself, not merely recurrence inferred from context.

Screen the full article inventory: uchi/aida/toki/kagiri may overlap for temporal conditions; ori/sai/toki overlap for occasions; baai can frame a case, tsuide a secondary errand, mae/ato event order, and goto recurrence. The visible task limits these formulations without branding them globally ungrammatical.

Coverage is constrained function/form practice, not unrestricted discrimination of all temporal nouns. Ori and sai have three model answers each within six shared occasion items, not six independently contrasted targets. Goro suffix production, every aida construction, all uchi uses and formal-notice honorific wording remain outside this batch.
